summary:
Field Twin | a digital twin of the farm

In 2026, farmers near Tomaszów Lubelski in eastern Poland reported bean losses of 95–98%, while the official drought app showed as little as 11% for some of them. The official system never looked at individual fields. NASA satellites watched them all season.

Field Twin turns NASA Earth observation data into a three-season plan for each field. It replays the season week by week, using rainfall (GPM IMERG), soil moisture (SMAP) and field-level greenness at 30 m (HLS). It then shows why a field lost: how many days it stood bare, whether it had a cover crop, and whether water drained away in ditches. From that diagnosis it builds a plan: a crop rotation that moves sensitive crops to fields that hold water, winter cover crops, sluices on ditches, reduced tillage and a flowering strip.

The plan pays for itself. Cover-crop subsidies and fertiliser savings return about 428–578 PLN per hectare after seed costs. The farmer also gets a field-by-field record of the season for insurers. Farms pay 15 PLN/ha a year, and the first 20 ha are free.

Our working web demo follows one composite farm built from real 2026 cases.
details:
What it does and how it works

Field Twin is a digital twin of a farm. It takes NASA Earth observation data and turns it into a three-season plan for each field: what to sow, how to keep water in the field, and what the plan earns.

The app has three screens:

  1. My season replays the 2026 season week by week for a single field. It shows rainfall (GPM IMERG, ~10 km), soil moisture (SMAP, ~9 km) and crop greenness (HLS, 30 m, field level) against the multi-year average, and marks the period when the loss began. Satellite views of the field before and after the loss make the damage visible at a glance.
  2. Why this field compares the farm’s fields. It shows how many days the soil stood bare, whether there was a cover crop, the slope, runoff and soil type, and the loss per field. Regional groundwater from GRACE-FO is shown as context, clearly labelled as regional, not field-level.
  3. My rotation builds a plan for 2027–2029. Sensitive crops move to the fields that hold water best, winters get cover crops, and the plan adds sluices on drainage ditches, reduced tillage, a flowering strip and a retention pond. For every step it shows the water effect, the cost and the money, and at the end it shows the plan’s net payback.

Benefits and intended impact

The farmer sees why a field failed and gets a concrete plan for the next three seasons. Cover-crop subsidies (437.60 PLN/ha in the 2025 campaign) and fertiliser savings (250–400 PLN/ha) mean the plan returns about 428–578 PLN per hectare after seed and sowing. Every field also gets a record of the season, which helps with insurance claims. That matters in a year when an official drought tool reported 11% losses on fields where farmers lost 95–98%.

Water retention, covered soil and flowering strips also help biodiversity. These benefits come with a plan that farmers adopt for economic reasons.

The business model: farms pay 15 PLN/ha a year, with the first 20 ha free. Farm advisors, insurers and banks are secondary customers. Next steps are a pilot with about 10 farms in Lubelskie in the 2027 season, then season records for insurers and other drought-hit regions of Poland in 2028.

Tools and technologies

[Frontend framework and language, e.g. React / Next.js, TypeScript], charts in [library], deployed on Vercel. Data sources: NASA HLS, SMAP, GPM IMERG, ECOSTRESS, GRACE-FO and POWER, plus partner data from ARiMR (field parcels and crop declarations), IUNG (soil and drought monitoring) and SoilGrids. [Data processing: language and tools, if any.] The demo uses prepared data for one composite farm. Water and yield figures are a model, not a guarantee.

What makes it creative

Most drought tools stop at “there is a drought in your region”. Field Twin goes from a satellite pixel to a decision on a single field, and from that decision to money. Every chart shows its own spatial scale, so the farmer knows what is measured at field level and what is regional. Crop rotation is the backbone of the plan, but the plan also covers water, soil and biodiversity measures, each with its cost and return.

Factors the team considered

  • Resolution honesty: SMAP and IMERG are too coarse for one field, so HLS carries the field-level signal and the coarser datasets provide context.
  • Timing: cover crops can only be sown after harvest, so the plan starts in 2027 rather than promising instant results.
  • Agronomy limits: the app recommends crop types, and an agronomist confirms the species and every step.
  • Who pays: the plan has to pay for itself through existing subsidies and savings, so the farmer has a reason to use it.
  • Farm size: the same logic works for a 20 ha family farm and a 200 ha business, and the free tier lowers the entry barrier.
